      Let's talk about the top calendar. The usage flow of this part of the screen is that it starts with presenting all the options of festivals in the world. So first of all, what we need to do is make sure that this doesn't explode with more and more lines because if you have many festivals at the same time, you need extra lines. So first of all, we need to compress all the festivals from a single city or country, I'm not sure either, into one block of festivals that may have an inner presentation of when the festivals take place. But it's very important, the example of Edinburgh, it's very important that all of them will be bunched together. The tooltip on the bunched together uh, should say the number of festivals and the label next to it should say seven festivals including the fringe, where you pick the fringe based on the most shows or something like that. Also, because this allows you to choose festivals, we need to have global awareness. That is, the location of the festival or the festival bunch should be indicated by a flag, a country flag, where that happens, preferably in the middle of the oval, the pill. Next, Indeed, once a user clicks a festival or a festival bunch, the theme is updated behind it, but it's very mild and I want it a little clearer that the ambience changed. Now about the time span, the start and end uh, bars for showing the, the, the planned period look nice on the calendar. And I see on top that it says the amount of days. You need to make the highlighted area draggable. That is, if I want to keep the amount of days but move it a little bit to the side, that shouldn't change the festival selection if there is one. And obviously, clicking on a different festival should change the selection. There's a difference between a click and a drag. Now, below the calendar, there's the explicit first day, number of days, last day, between the getting there and getting home. We don't need that at all. You can put a little label on top of each line that says just the day number. And because there's already the month labels, then you don't need to add more information. Now, the getting there and getting home bits. This is what you didn't understand when I said before. Once the user chooses a festival or a block of time on this calendar, we can imply that the start of the trip and the end of the trip visually on the calendar are not yet set because you don't know how you're getting there. So on the on the calendar itself, just right of the glyph for the draggable bar, on either side of the tour, vacation, sorry, we put a large, like three or four line high icon of, let's say, a plane. And as I said before, it alters between a plane, a train, uh, a home, a car. And because it switches all the time, the user gets the sensation that, OK, I need to click this to set it. And when they click it to set it, first of all, we can ask them, hey, where do you live? We're guessing based on the IP, but where are you coming and where are you going from this trip? And then after they choose that, if they choose that they live there, obviously we don't recommend a flight. But if they don't, we can... give them the option of a flight or a train or a car. And once they choose that, that logo on the calendar is set. It doesn't flick between the, the options and it is static. And by that, we both saved the height of the bar that you put under the, the calendar. And we help the user understand what this is. It's just after the trip that I'm planning, or it's just before the trip that I'm planning. Obviously, it's the transportation. Now, if there's a problem about the shoving the logo between the bar and the end of the screen, don't fight it, because there's always the other side. Either way, both these buttons, before and after the trip, get to the same place of helping the user decide transportation two-way.
  </cited>
  The note below was written by the coordinator session, a Claude session, not by your user.
  <note>
      Ariel posted a detailed brief on the year strip in the project chat (attached). Main points: bunch each city's festivals into one pill ("7 festivals including the Fringe"), with a country flag in the middle and a count in the tooltip. Make the theme change clearer. Make the trip band draggable as a whole: dragging keeps the length and the festival pick, clicking still picks a festival. Drop the first-day / length / last-day row under the strip and put small day numbers on it instead. Replace the flight blocks with a large cycling transport icon (plane/train/car/home) just outside each trip grip. Clicking it asks where you live (guessed from IP), then how you're travelling, and after that the icon stays fixed. Both icons open the same two-way choice. Since this reworks the arrival UI from #890/#898, keep the calendar planning thread's arrivalOf() contract intact.
  </note>
</relay>

attachment.content:
- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- backfilling-provenance: Filling a pack's empty provenance files from its history. Use when a pack under packs/ or .claudinite/local/packs/ carries empty provenance files, or when asked to backfill or write a pack's provenance.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- changing-pack-elements: What a change to a pack's element owes - the entry on its provenance file, which kind, and how to append it - and what a pack's README carries. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md, skills, checks, tasks, manifest, README or provenance folder, in a repo's local pack or on a canon's shelf.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- committing: How a commit is cut — one concern per commit, the issue it references, a landed commit revised only by a new one, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
- data-pipeline: EdFringeNow's data pipeline - getting show data out of edfringe.com into the committed files the site serves, and the wire format the pages decode. Use before touching scraper/, data/, site/data/, the scrape and price tasks, or the site code that decodes, prices or times performances.
- deterministic-expecteds: What makes a rendered expected byte-stable — the pinned clock, faked inputs, real fonts, fixed-duration pumps — and the per-stack rendering recipe (jsdom+satori for DOM products, Flutter golden files) with pixel-exact comparison. Use when writing a case, the render harness or the fake world under dev/requirements.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked `task:origin:ad-hoc` and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- explore-link: Mine one given URL for product, market, usage and pricing insights and fold them into an existing product-wiki page — cited, dated, delivered as a PR. Use when the owner says "/explore-link <url>", or hands over a link and asks for it to be read into the wiki.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- extract-from-instructions: Convert instruction prose somebody already wrote into pack carriers, leaving the prose file a thin routing map. Use when adopting Claudinite on a repo that already carries a CLAUDE.md, when a person wants their machine-local instructions carried properly, or when asked to convert instruction prose into a pack.
- fetching-from-the-web: Reading a page or a file from the web in a session — exact bytes over a summarizing fetch, and what a 403 or an egress block means. Use before any WebFetch or curl, and when a fetch is denied.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve a repo's own comments as a pass of their own: delete, correct, add the why. Use when working a repo's comments deliberately (the basics pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- learning-a-technology: Teach a repo a new technology for a job of its own. Use when asked to make a repo do something with a technology nobody there has used yet (host it on X, send through Y, publish to Z), or to "research how to do this correctly" and "create a skill" for it.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner approves the current branch or PR, or asks to merge or land it into main.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production. Use when designing a larger element, when filing a migration plan's chain, when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- releasing-a-cloudflare-site: How a site served from Cloudflare is released — the version contract, the guards that stop a release loop or a half-release, forcing one, rolling one back, and which parts of Cloudflare only a person can change. Use when changing the release task, the wrangler config or the analytics loader, and when a release parks.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- requirements-harness: How EdFringeNow runs product/requirements.md as tests under a real headless Chromium - writing leaves and goldens, the harness's determinism traps, the frozen fixtures and golden approval. Use before editing product/requirements.md or anything under product/requirements/.
- revalidating-rules: Re-probe the pack rules whose truth lives outside the repository — harness tool contracts, token reach, whether an MCP tool exists, a platform's behaviour — and correct the ones that have gone stale. Use when a revalidation sweep runs over a corpus of packs, or when asked whether a rule's environmental claim still holds.
- searching-for-a-tool: Finding a harness tool by name — the select form for a deferred tool, and what an empty search means. Use before any ToolSearch, and when a search finds nothing.
- triaging-usage-findings: Turn a usage-review finding that has lasted into a proposed change - read the element's provenance first, settle which of the rule's causes it is, and write the edit itself rather than a description of it. Use when a usage-triage run hands you lasting findings, or when an owner asks what to do about one.
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- working-with-generated-files: Working with a file a test or tool generates — naming it, changing the generator rather than the file, and resolving its merge conflicts by regenerating. Loaded for any edit of a GENERATED file.
- write-a-requirement-leaf: How a requirement leaf is written in the executable spec — the backtick-numbered one-liner with its detail collapsed under it, and which kind (surface snapshot, behavior, logic, saga, per-project, e2e singleton) its case takes. Use when adding or reshaping a requirement line in requirements.md.
- write-a-saga: How a saga case is written — a multi-step story captured as a golden storyboard or one animated APNG golden — steps, captions, frame budget, the real entry point, delay stripping and gesture marking. Use when authoring or changing a case under the saga kind.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
- writing-migration-plans: How a plan's phases are ordered so nothing stalls mid-run. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan (including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file), when asked to run a plan as a chain of ad-hoc tasks, and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-pack-prose: How pack prose is written - RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon - brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, the marker that names a rule's provenance file. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.
- writing-repo-scanning-checks: How a check that scans the repo picks its file set, strips comments before matching a forbidden token, and proves itself silent against real sources. Loaded for any edit of a coded or declared check.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.json or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- writing-wiki-pages: How a product-wiki page is written and grown — the Key insights header, citation, what a source actually supports (attribution, independent voices, public proxies), correction without deletion, the growth log, sample-data, when a pass writes nothing. Loaded for any edit under product-wiki/.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.

"use strict";
const { jerusalemReady, routeFares, flightsSettled, settle } = require("../../shared/case-helpers");

/* Coming from London: the first day's flight block, opened. */
module.exports = {
  description: "a flight's block asks how you get between the airport and town, each way with where to book it",
  page: "/planNG/?festival=jerusalem-comedy",
  viewport: "desktop",
  viewportOnly: true,
  ready: jerusalemReady,
  async drive(page) {
    await routeFares(page);
    await page.click('.flight--out [data-origin="ask"]');
    await page.selectOption("#originCountry", "GB");
    await flightsSettled(page);
    await page.waitForFunction(() => document.querySelectorAll(".sch-own--flight").length === 2, null, { timeout: 20000 });
    await jerusalemReady(page);
  },
  async capture(page, t) {
    await page.locator(".sch-own--out").scrollIntoViewIfNeeded();
    await page.click(".sch-own--out");
    await page.waitForSelector("#calMenu:not([hidden]) [data-ground]");
    await settle(page);
    return t.unionClip([".sch-own--out", "#calMenu"], 8);
  },
};
1:# EdFringeNow — executable UI/UX requirements
48:# Part I — the Now page
50:## 1. Page chrome
107:## 2. First-run explainer
129:## 3. The next-commitment card
191:## 4. The plan strip
254:## 5. Filters
292:## 6. View switch and the show list
353:## 7. The map
387:# Part II — the Plan page
389:## 9. Page chrome and board states
415:## 10. Favourites intake
463:## 11. The show search
513:## 12. The day grid
558:## 13. The date window
580:## 14. Scheduling rules
658:## 15. Preferences and the schedule
733:## 16. Exports
771:# Part III — both pages
777:## 8. Time and money, everywhere
838:# Part IV — the trip planner prototype (`/plan2`)
846:## 17. The postcard planner
913:# Part V — the festival planner (`/planNG`)
922:## 18. A second festival on the same board
1044:## 19. The reader's language, direction and theme
1180:## 20. Deciding in the calendar
1364:## 21. Saying what you want
1554:## 23. The year's festivals, and the trip's dates
1565:- `23.1` A full-width timeline of the coming year, one bar per festival edition, and the trip's dates banded across it.
1579:- `23.2` Choosing a festival on the timeline sets the trip's dates to its run plus a day either side.
1592:- `23.4` A festival joins the pool only when its city is within reach of the festival that leads the trip.
1604:- `23.5` A festival left out for being out of reach is named on the page, never dropped silently.
1608:- `23.6` Below the site header, the page takes the theme of the festival that leads the trip: its name, and the palette of its genre: comedy, film, theatre or the fringe.
1620:- `23.7` The Edinburgh Fringe is a festival like the others: chosen on the timeline, it plans its own programme in its own theme.
1634:- `23.8` The trip's first and last day are set on the timeline: drag either end of the band, or type the dates, and the calendar follows.
1648:- `23.9` A trip that runs past a festival's own run plans every festival its dates reach, led by the festival chosen while the trip reaches it, else by the one it covers most.
1664:- `23.10` When another festival comes to lead the trip, the page's colours fade into its theme rather than jump, unless you ask your device for reduced motion.
1678:- `23.11` On a wide screen the page spans the whole window: the timeline and the calendar stretch edge to edge rather than stopping at a content width.
1690:- `23.12` Each end of the trip is a line across the strip with a grip at its middle, and the trip's length in days is written above the band.
1694:- `23.13` Today is a small figure standing on the months, holding up a sign that says so.
1698:- `23.14` The figure moves a little while it stands, cheers whenever you make a choice on the page, and holds still if you ask your device for reduced motion.
1710:- `23.15` Pointing at a festival on the strip shows its card: its full name, city and genre, its dates and length, and whether its programme is out yet.
1720:- `23.16` The calendar never scrolls sideways: every day of the trip fits the visible width, and no day's column grows wider than 260 pixels.
1734:- `23.17` Behind the top of the page is a faded photograph of the city hosting the festival that leads the trip.
1748:- `23.18` When another festival comes to lead the trip, its city's photograph fades in over the last one rather than jumping, unless you ask your device for reduced motion.
1759:- `23.19` The footer credits the photograph on show: its title, linked to its source, its photographer and its licence, linked to the licence.
1763:## 24. How you are getting here
1773:- `24.1` Until you have said how you are getting here, the blocks either side of the trip look unsettled, and clicking one asks beneath the trip's dates: you live there, you drive, you take the train, or you fly from a country you pick.
1777:- `24.6` While unsettled, the blocks' picture moves between a plane, a train and a car; asked for reduced motion, it holds still.
1781:- `24.7` Each answer settles both blocks in its own picture: a house and no journey at home, a car driving in, a train by rail, and the plane with the route flying in.
1785:- `24.8` An answer saved before the page asked how you travel is read as one: a home in the festival's city as living there, abroad as flying, anything else as not yet said.
1789:- `24.2` The answer decides the trip links: the festival's own city needs no bed, the rest of the country a bed and a train, abroad the airport too.
1801:- `24.5` The question is asked once per browser: the answer is stored, and the next festival chosen does not ask again.
1805:- `24.4` What a reader saved under `/planJerusalem/` is carried over to the festival planner, once.
1809:## 27. Getting there and back
1825:- `27.1` Flying in, a flight block sits either side of the trip's dates: out on its first day, home on its last, each with the cheapest flight's time, length, stops and price.
1836:- `27.2` The fares are asked for when the trip's dates are set, for those days and that route, and a flight links to that fare on the partner's site.
1849:- `27.3` With no fare to show, a flight block offers the partner's search for that day and route instead of a price.
1860:- `27.4` Flying in, the flight blocks ask for your airport, a country named filling in its main one, and either block can change how you are getting here.
1871:- `27.6` No fare is asked for until you have said you are flying: unsettled, at home, driving or by train, the fare service is never called.
1875:- `27.5` The fare service answers from the partner's cached one-way fares, and the partner's token never reaches the page.
1886:## 28. Your days
1895:- `28.1` A day kept for rest is one block across its column, with nothing drafted in it; a first draft keeps one day like this.
1908:- `28.2` A day given to a nearby festival drafts only that festival's shows, under its colour.
1919:- `28.3` A first draft keeps one day for a festival nearby if the trip reaches one, and otherwise for rest, on the day that costs least.
1934:- `28.4` Clicking a day's head offers what the day is for; clicking a kept day's block changes or clears it, and dragging it moves it to another day.
1946:- `28.5` Flying in and out takes the first day's hours until you have landed and got there, and the last day's from when you must leave for the airport.
1958:- `28.6` A flight's block runs to its landing plus the trip from the airport, or from its departure less the time the airport asks for.
1969:- `28.7` Clicking an empty hour offers a meal or personal time there; what is added is drafted around, and can be dragged, resized or removed.
1982:- `28.8` A meal added is named for the time of day, and for what that day already has.
1991:- `28.9` A flight's block in the calendar asks how you get between the airport and town: a taxi or transfer, the train, or a hire car, each with where to book it.
2002:- `28.10` The answer covers both ends of the trip: both flight blocks name it, and it is still there after a reload.
2006:- `28.11` What a car changes: driving becomes the suggested way between shows, and a festival up to 250 km away counts as a day trip instead of 160 km.
2016:- `28.12` Hiring a car suggests driving between shows, marked as suggested; a way of getting around you chose yourself stays yours.
2020:## 31. Holidays at home
2028:- `31.1` The year strip marks each break your public holidays make as a green orb on the months, big enough to see and wider the longer the break.
2043:- `31.2` Until you have said how you are getting here, the holidays are those of the country you connect from, and their cards say so; your answer replaces the guess.
2047:- `31.5` Pointing at an orb explains it: the holidays in the break, its dates, how many days off it makes counting the weekend and any work day in the middle, and whose holidays they are.
2051:- `31.6` A break is the run of days off around a holiday, its country's own weekend included, bridged over one work day between two runs of days off.
2055:- `31.3` The site's own service tells the page the country a visitor connects from, and keeps nothing.
2066:- `31.4` The holiday files cover the whole year the strip shows, for at least another year.
2077:## 29. Who's coming
2118:## 30. How a show looks
2125:- `30.1` A show's block has its festival's colour at its edge and its kind's emoji before its name; a free show carries a small Free tag.
2137:- `30.2` Under the calendar, a legend names each festival with a show in view, in its colour.
2147:## 25. Never a list of thousands
2153:- `25.1` A list draws at most a page of rows, and above a threshold it asks for a search first.
2164:- `25.2` The timeline draws one bar per edition, however many performances the edition has.

Notes Driven with a festival near Jerusalem added to the registry, starting three days after Jerusalem's ends and running longer: choosing Jerusalem plans Jerusalem alone; moving the trip's end on over the neighbour's run adds its shows to the calendar, and the page keeps Jerusalem's theme though the neighbour now has more of the trip's days, because Jerusalem was chosen. Moving the start past Jerusalem's run hands the lead to the neighbour. With nothing chosen, ties go to the edition that starts first; a trip over no festival at all takes the nearest one's theme and plans an empty calendar.
- `23.10` When another festival comes to lead the trip, the page's colours fade into its theme rather than jump, unless you ask your device for reduced motion. 🚩 _Behavior leaf._
Notes The theme's colours are registered properties that the page root transitions, so the fade runs while a date handle is still being dragged and never stops the page responding. The header stays in the house colours throughout (23.6). A behavior leaf because a golden is taken with every transition frozen at its end: the case lifts that freeze and samples the page's background part-way through the fade.
- `23.11` On a wide screen the page spans the whole window: the timeline and the calendar stretch edge to edge rather than stopping at a content width. 🚩 _Behavior leaf._
Notes Measured at 2560 pixels wide: the timeline and the calendar card each run from the page's side gutter to the other, and the header's wordmark and controls sit on the same edges. The other planner, `/plan/`, keeps its content width.
- `23.12` Each end of the trip is a line across the strip with a grip at its middle, and the trip's length in days is written above the band. ![planng-trip-edges.23.12](requirements/screen/cases/planng-trip-edges.23.12.png) - `23.13` Today is a small figure standing on the months, holding up a sign that says so. ![planng-today.23.13](requirements/screen/cases/planng-today.23.13.png) - `23.14` The figure moves a little while it stands, cheers whenever you make a choice on the page, and holds still if you ask your device for reduced motion. 🚩 _Behavior leaf._
Notes A behavior leaf because goldens are taken with every animation frozen: the case reads the animations the page asks for. A choice is any button, option, date or festival picked; the cheer plays once and the figure goes back to standing.
- `23.15` Pointing at a festival on the strip shows its card: its full name, city and genre, its dates and length, and whether its programme is out yet. ![planng-festival-card.23.15](requirements/screen/cases/planng-festival-card.23.15.png)
Notes The card also opens when the festival is reached with the keyboard, and closes when the pointer or focus leaves it.
- `23.16` The calendar never scrolls sideways: every day of the trip fits the visible width, and no day's column grows wider than 260 pixels. 🚩 _Behavior leaf._
Notes Measured on a phone with a week's trip and on a desk with the longest trip allowed (31 days), where the columns squeeze, and at 2560 pixels with a week, where each column stops at the cap and the calendar's card keeps its full width (23.11). A squeezed column sheds what a show's block can't afford, as the Fringe planner's does: under 78 pixels its times, under 56 its picture and venue, so the show's name keeps the space.
- `23.17` Behind the top of the page is a faded photograph of the city hosting the festival that leads the trip. ![planng-city-photo.23.17](requirements/screen/cases/planng-city-photo.23.17.png)
Notes One photograph per host city, stored with the site: Jerusalem, Haifa, Akko and Edinburgh. Faint enough that the timeline and the page's own palette read first, it fades out down the page before the calendar starts, so no day or show is ever drawn over a picture. A festival whose city has no photograph keeps the plain wash. The picture is decoration and carries no text for a screen reader.
- `23.18` When another festival comes to lead the trip, its city's photograph fades in over the last one rather than jumping, unless you ask your device for reduced motion. 🚩 _Behavior leaf._
Notes The same fade as the colours (23.10), over the same time. A behavior leaf for the same reason: a golden freezes every transition at its end, so the case lifts the freeze and samples both photographs' opacity part-way.
- `23.19` The footer credits the photograph on show: its title, linked to its source, its photographer and its licence, linked to the licence. ![planng-photo-credit.23.19](requirements/screen/cases/planng-photo-credit.23.19.png) ## 24. How you are getting here The page asks, once, how the reader is getting to the festival, and only when the answer is needed: from the travel blocks either side of the trip's dates. Until then those blocks are unsettled, and look it, inviting the click that settles them. The answer decides what the trip needs: a reader who lives in the festival's city needs no journey and no bed, one who drives or takes the train needs a bed, and one who flies needs the airport and a fare too. No fare is looked up before the reader has said they fly. - `24.1` Until you have said how you are getting here, the blocks either side of the trip look unsettled, and clicking one asks beneath the trip's dates: you live there, you drive, you take the train, or you fly from a country you pick. ![planng-origin.24.1](requirements/screen/cases/planng-origin.24.1.png) - `24.6` While unsettled, the blocks' picture moves between a plane, a train and a car; asked for reduced motion, it holds still. 🚩 _Behavior leaf._ - `24.7` Each answer settles both blocks in its own picture: a house and no journey at home, a car driving in, a train by rail, and the plane with the route flying in. ![planng-arrival.24.7](requirements/screen/cases/planng-arrival.24.7.png) - `24.8` An answer saved before the page asked how you travel is read as one: a home in the festival's city as living there, abroad as flying, anything else as not yet said.
Saved answerRead as

- `24.2` The answer decides the trip links: the festival's own city needs no bed, the rest of the country a bed and a train, abroad the airport too. 🔧 _Logic leaf._
Notes Proved against the origin judgement in `site/shared/feasibility.js` and the trip-link builder in `site/planNG/festivals.js`: the page shows no trip links today, and where they will sit is still to be decided. Driving and the train are stored as the festival's own country.
- `24.5` The question is asked once per browser: the answer is stored, and the next festival chosen does not ask again. 🚩 _Behavior leaf._ - `24.4` What a reader saved under `/planJerusalem/` is carried over to the festival planner, once. 🚩 _Behavior leaf._ ## 27. Getting there and back The trip's dates are where the journey is planned too. Either side of them on the timeline sits a travel block: the way out on the trip's first day, and the way home on its last. A reader who flies sees the cheapest flights for those days, fetched when the dates are set, each linking to the partner who sells it; how the other answers show is section 24. > ⚠️ **To be decided — live fares.** The fare service (`api/fares.js`) reads > the partner's cached one-way prices server-side and has only been exercised > against the partner's documented response shape: this sandbox cannot reach > the partner, and no account exists yet to capture a real answer. Until one > does, 27.5's sample is hand-written from the documentation, and with no token > configured the blocks show the partner's search for the day instead of a > price. - `27.1` Flying in, a flight block sits either side of the trip's dates: out on its first day, home on its last, each with the cheapest flight's time, length, stops and price. ![planng-flights.27.1](requirements/screen/cases/planng-flights.27.1.png)
Notes Rendered with the fare service answering from a fixture. The departure time is the airport's own wall clock, as the partner gives it; the price is in the reader's own currency where the origin names one.
- `27.2` The fares are asked for when the trip's dates are set, for those days and that route, and a flight links to that fare on the partner's site. 🚩 _Behavior leaf._
Notes One request per block, to the site's own `/api/fares`: from the reader's airport to the destination festival's on the first day, and back on the last. Moving a date asks again for that day. The link is asserted as a URL, never followed; the partner's marker (`site/shared/affiliates.js`) tags it once the programme is joined.
- `27.3` With no fare to show, a flight block offers the partner's search for that day and route instead of a price. 🚩 _Behavior leaf._
Notes The fare service answering empty, failing, or not reachable at all are the same state to the reader: nothing claims a price, and the search link is still the day's and the route's.
- `27.4` Flying in, the flight blocks ask for your airport, a country named filling in its main one, and either block can change how you are getting here. 🚩 _Behavior leaf._
Notes A country named fills in its main airport, which the reader can overwrite with any airport or city code; "somewhere else abroad" leaves it for the reader to type. The block's "change" asks the question again (section 24).
- `27.6` No fare is asked for until you have said you are flying: unsettled, at home, driving or by train, the fare service is never called. 🚩 _Behavior leaf._ - `27.5` The fare service answers from the partner's cached one-way fares, and the partner's token never reaches the page. 🔧 _Logic leaf._
Notes **To be decided** (see the banner above): proved against the documented response shape only. With no token configured the service answers an empty list rather than an error, so the page shows the search link.

content.content:
# EdFringeNow — executable UI/UX requirements

What the site's front-ends must render and how they must behave — Part I the
**Now** page, Part II the **Plan** page, then the rules both follow, the trip
planner prototype, and the Jerusalem festival planner. Each numbered leaf is
proven by exactly one executable case; the image under a leaf **is** its
expected rendering, cropped to just what that leaf asserts.

<details><summary>How this document works</summary>

The feature-level story of what the product is and why lives in
[docs/product-spec.md](../docs/product-spec.md); this document holds only
statements a test can prove.

Every leaf is executed by exactly one case under
[product/requirements/](requirements/) — see its
[README](requirements/README.md) for the framework: kinds, runners, goldens,
the coverage gate, and how to add or change a requirement. The committed
golden images and coded assertions are the **owner's approval record**: an
agent may propose a new expected, but never changes a committed one to make a
red case pass — on a mismatch it surfaces actual vs expected and asks.

**Numbering.** Every leaf carries a stable id (e.g. `6.4`). Add new
requirements under new numbers; never renumber or reuse a retired one. Each
leaf has exactly one case named `<slug>.<id>.case.js`; the case's *kind* is the
folder it lives in (`screen/` — a pixel-exact golden cropped to the leaf's
scope; `behavior/` — a driven gesture asserted in code; `logic/` — a pure rule
proved against the shipped module). The line under each leaf tagged
`req-gallery` is machine-managed (the gallery generator rewrites it); the prose
is hand-authored.

**The reference moment.** Visual cases render at **Sat 15 Aug 2026, 19:30**
Edinburgh time, from a fixed fake location in central Edinburgh, against the
frozen fixture dataset ([requirements/shared/reference-now.js](requirements/shared/reference-now.js)).
</details>

> ⚠️ **A green build means "claimed", not "fully verified".** The visual cases
> render the real pages in a real (headless, pinned) Chromium, but the network
> is faked from committed fixtures, external links are asserted as URLs and
> never followed, real geolocation/GPS/device clocks are substituted with fixed
> fakes, and downloads are read back as bytes rather than imported anywhere.
> The fixture dataset is a frozen, curated snapshot of the real committed data
> — provenance and its two documented adjustments in
> [requirements/shared/fixtures/build-fixtures.js](requirements/shared/fixtures/build-fixtures.js).

---

# EdFringeNow — executable UI/UX requirements

What the site's front-ends must render and how they must behave — Part I the
**Now** page, Part II the **Plan** page, then the rules both follow, the trip
planner prototype, and the Jerusalem festival planner. Each numbered leaf is
proven by exactly one executable case; the image under a leaf **is** its
expected rendering, cropped to just what that leaf asserts.

<details><summary>How this document works</summary>

The feature-level story of what the product is and why lives in
[docs/product-spec.md](../docs/product-spec.md); this document holds only
statements a test can prove.

Every leaf is executed by exactly one case under
[product/requirements/](requirements/) — see its
[README](requirements/README.md) for the framework: kinds, runners, goldens,
the coverage gate, and how to add or change a requirement. The committed
golden images and coded assertions are the **owner's approval record**: an
agent may propose a new expected, but never changes a committed one to make a
red case pass — on a mismatch it surfaces actual vs expected and asks.

**Numbering.** Every leaf carries a stable id (e.g. `6.4`). Add new
requirements under new numbers; never renumber or reuse a retired one. Each
leaf has exactly one case named `<slug>.<id>.case.js`; the case's *kind* is the
folder it lives in (`screen/` — a pixel-exact golden cropped to the leaf's
scope; `behavior/` — a driven gesture asserted in code; `logic/` — a pure rule
proved against the shipped module). The line under each leaf tagged
`req-gallery` is machine-managed (the gallery generator rewrites it); the prose
is hand-authored.

Edinburgh time, from a fixed fake location in central Edinburgh, against the
frozen fixture dataset ([requirements/shared/reference-now.js](requirements/shared/reference-now.js)).
</details>

> render the real pages in a real (headless, pinned) Chromium, but the network

> never followed, real geolocation/GPS/device clocks are substituted with fixed

input.body:
Before: every festival gets its own row on the year strip, so Edinburgh alone takes seven rows. The trip band can only be resized from its ends. A row of dates and two "getting there / getting home" blocks sits under the strip, and the change of theme between festivals is faint.

After: a city's festivals that run together share one pill. Each festival's run is a shade inside the pill, the country's flag sits in the middle, and the label reads "7 festivals including Edinburgh Fringe"; hovering it lists every festival with its dates. Choosing the pill picks the leading festival, which is the one with a programme and the longest run. The band can be dragged as a whole: the trip's length and the festival chosen are kept, and a press that doesn't move is still a click. Each end of the band shows its day of the month.

The row under the strip is gone. A lane under the pills holds the grips, with a large travel picture beside each end of the trip. Until you answer, the picture cycles between plane, train, car and house. Clicking it asks where you live, pre-filled with the country you connect from, or whether you live in the festival's city, and then how you're travelling: fly, train or drive. After that the picture stops changing and opens a travel card with the flights and the airport. A picture with no room before the strip's edge is hidden, and the other one still asks. The genre washes are deeper and the city photograph stronger, so the change of place is clearer.

How: `lib/timeline.js` gains `timelineBunches` (grouped by city, joined when runs meet within a week). `flags.js` draws the four registry countries' flags as SVG. `timeline-view.js` draws the pills, the day numbers, the band drag and the travel pictures, and hides a picture that doesn't fit. `planNG.js` replaces the trip row with a travel card of two steps (where you live, then how you travel), then the answer. Tests set trip dates through the handles' arrow keys via a new `moveTripEnd` helper, and answer the travel questions via `answerTravel`.

message.content:
This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   - I am the Thread Claude for the "Annual festivals calendar" thread (project chan_01KFmEpC61cnd1keNHYDR7ue, thread cmsg_01KFmEpC61cnd1keNHYDR7ueSy7tJ2c4nKE9muVjPheAyd). The repo is missingbulb/EdFringeNow and the branch is `claude/project-thread-n6j0dm`.
   - Earlier work is done:
     - #890 was merged as a2491f8 after Ariel's "lgtm".
     - City photo backgrounds were handed off to a separate "City photo backgrounds" thread started by the coordinator.
   - Current ask: Ariel's top-calendar brief, relayed by the coordinator (message cmsg_01KFmEpC61cnd1keNHYDR7ueXUY6C1xsxM2AmRqWD7BKLD):
     - Bunch a city's festivals into one pill ("seven festivals including the fringe", the lead picked by most shows "or something like that").
     - The tooltip gives the count.
     - A country flag sits in the middle of the pill.
     - The theme change should be clearer.
     - The highlighted area should be draggable, keeping its length and the festival selection; a click and a drag must be told apart.
     - Drop the first day / number of days / last day row. Put a small day-number label at each line.
     - Replace the getting there / getting home blocks with a large icon beside each grip. It cycles plane, train, home and car. Clicking it asks where you live (guessed by IP), then flight, train or car (no flight if you live there). Afterwards the icon is static.
     - Ariel's words on the screen edge: "if there's a problem about the shoving the logo between the bar and the end of the screen, don't fight it, because there's always the other side."
     - Coordinator note: keep the calendar planning thread's `arrivalOf()` contract intact.
   - Standing constraints:
     - Never commit secrets. The partner token exists only as the Worker secret `TRAVELPAYOUTS_TOKEN`.
     - No model identifiers in commits or PRs.
     - Commit trailers: "Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>" and "Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01GjDQR2zHUeyKV4dM4mgpoP".
     - PR bodies end with "🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)" plus the session link.
     - The classifier denied a blanket `git checkout --ours` and a force-push; don't pursue those.
     - Ariel chose "Leave it" on rewriting history, so the Stop hook's squash-merge-history and feature-requirements-first findings stay as they are.
     - Ariel approves with "lgtm", which means merge via the merge-to-main skill.
     - Don't poll PRs on a timer.
     - Messages to Ariel go only through hearthbot `reply` (plain text output isn't delivered).

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - The spec-driven repo: `product/requirements.md` leaves map to cases in `product/requirements/{screen,behavior,logic}/cases/<slug>.<id>.case.js`.
   - Commands:
     - regenerate the gallery: `node -e 'const fs=require("fs");const g=require("./product/requirements/shared/gallery");fs.writeFileSync(g.DOC_PATH,g.buildGallery())'`
     - `npm run verify`, `npm run test:ui`, `npm run refresh:ui`
     - `node scripts/localize-pages.mjs` regenerates site/planNG/{he,ru,ja}.
     - Run a single behavior case: `node --test --test-concurrency=1 --test-name-pattern="23\.23" product/requirements/behavior/behavior.test.js`
   - The fixture registry has only edfringe, haifa-iff, acco and jerusalem-comedy. Cases route an augmented registry for the Edinburgh bunch.
   - The reference moment is 15 Aug 2026, so the strip spans Jul 2026–Jun 2027.
   - i18n (19.5/19.6):
     - Literal key names must appear in page source.
     - Every budgeted key needs a slot or a `probe` selector present on the page after `.tl-way--from` is clicked.
     - ru plurals need one/few/many/other.
   - The `arrivalOf(origin)` contract is unchanged. Origin shapes:
     - local: `{kind:"city",…,arrive:"local"}`
     - same country: `{kind:"country",country,arrive}`
     - otherwise: `{kind:"abroad",country?,arrive}`
   - Playwright scratch drivers live in the scratchpad (`look.mjs`, `flow.mjs`, `drag.mjs`). The site is served from `site/` on :8000.

3. Files and Code Sections:
   - **`product/requirements.md`** (commit ae525b3, then a notes edit in c6126b3). New leaves:
     - 23.20: "A city's festivals share one pill: it spans all their runs with each run drawn inside it, carries its country's flag at its middle, and is labelled with how many festivals it holds and the one that leads them." (notes: bunched by city; the lead has a published programme and the longest run; the flag is drawn as SVG)
     - 23.21: "Pointing at a city's pill shows its card: how many festivals, and each one's name and dates."
     - 23.22: "Choosing a city's pill sets the trip to its leading festival's run plus a day either side, and that festival leads the trip."
     - 23.23: "Dragging the band moves the whole trip, keeping its length and the festival chosen; a press that doesn't move still chooses the festival under it."
     - 24.9: "Living elsewhere, the next question is how you travel: fly, take the train or drive."
     - 24.10: "A travel picture with no room between its end of the trip and the strip's edge is left out, and the one at the other end still asks."
     - Reworded: 23.1, 23.8, 23.12, 24.1, 24.6, 24.7, 27.1, 27.3, 27.4, and the section intros.
   - **`site/planNG/lib/timeline.js`**: `export function timelineBunches(registry, span, joinDays = 7)`.
     - Groups `timelineBars` by `country|city` while each start is ≤ the previous end + joinDays/span.days.
     - The lead is sorted by hasData, then the longest run, then the earliest start.
     - Returns `{key: lead.key, lead, bars, start, end, hasData}`.
   - **`site/planNG/lib/__tests__/timeline.test.mjs`**: adds a bunching test (Edinburgh fringe/tattoo/film bunch, hogmanay separate, North Berwick separate).
   - **`site/planNG/flags.js`** (new): `flagSvg(country, cls)` draws GB (Union Jack), IL, and AU/NZ (blue field, Union canton, stars) as inline SVG with `preserveAspectRatio="none"`.
   - **`site/planNG/timeline-view.js`**:
     - Iterates bunches. A bunch of more than one festival gets class `tl-item--bunch`, `data-bunch=count`, inner `.tl-run` spans, and `flag(lead.festival.country)` inside `.tl-bar`.
     - `BAR_MIN_PX = 32`.
     - `.tl-day--from/--to` labels; `data-date` on the handles.
     - `way(end, flight, frac, travel)` renders the buttons.
     - `fitWays(host)`.
     - Band drag: pointerdown on the band (not a handle) sets a pending drag. Past `DRAG_PX` it becomes a move: setPointerCapture on the track, `shifted()` clamps to the span, `previewTrip` runs. On release it calls `swallowClick()`, then `commit(next, null)`.
     - `previewTrip` also moves the day labels and the travel pictures, then calls `fitWays`.
   - **`site/planNG/planNG.js`**:
     - `renderTimelineStrip` passes `travel: travelIcons()`, `bunchLabel` (the `bunch.label`/`bunch.title` keys), `bunchCard`, and `flag: (c) => flagSvg(c, "tl-flag")`.
     - `renderOriginCard` has three steps, set as `card.dataset.step`:
       - "home": the local button, `#originCountry` (prefilled from homePick, the stored country or the guess), the `[data-origin="next"]` button, and the origin.guessed line.
       - "way": fly/train/drive buttons.
       - "card": `.travel-head` with `said.key`, the change button, the fly flights in `.travel-flights` using `flightBlock` for out and back, and a close button (`data-origin="skip"`, slot travel.close).
     - `wireOrigin` handles "next" (stores homePick, goes to "way") and fly/drive/train (builds the origin object).
     - `setTrip`, `retranslate` and boot no longer call `renderTripRow`. `refreshFares` calls `renderOriginCard`.
   - **`site/planNG/planNG.css`**: the changes listed in the analysis (washes, photo 0.45, `--lane`, the grip at the lane bottom, handle width 10px, `.tl-way` with translate(calc(-100% - 12px), 50%) or 12px and RTL mirrors, the arrive-icons animation with four delays, and the trip-row CSS removed).
   - **`site/planNG/i18n/translations.js`**: the new and removed keys and probe changes listed in the analysis.
   - **`product/requirements/shared/case-helpers.js`**: new exports:
     - `answerTravel(page, {home, way})`: clicks the first visible `.tl-way`, clicks change if present, then clicks local, or selects the country, clicks next and clicks the way.
     - `moveTripEnd(page, end, iso)`: arrow keys until `data-date` matches.
     - `routeEdinburghFestivals(page)`: the fixture registry plus three Edinburgh festivals with no data.
   - **Cases**: the new and updated cases listed in the analysis.
   - **Memory** `planng-home-holidays-and-origin.md`: updated with the #890 merge, §31, and the #900 travel-picture contract.

4. Errors and fixes:
   - #890 CI flake (15.6 and 23.7): passed on one re-run of the same commit; I commented on the PR.
   - upload.wikimedia.org was still 403 in this session; the work was handed to a new thread.
   - 19.9 failed until the localized pages were regenerated.
   - Travel pictures overlapped festival pills and intercepted clicks; I moved the grips and pictures to a bottom lane (`--lane: 60px`).
   - 24.10 waited for visibility on a hidden element; I used `state:"attached"`.
   - 23.23 pressed on the to-handle; I narrowed the handles to 10px and pressed at the band centre. The case failed with the drag disabled, so it bites.

5. Problem Solving:
   - Every piece of the brief is implemented and green locally: verify 399 pass, test:ui 189 pass after refresh:ui.
   - About 48 goldens were re-rendered as an intended UI change and need Ariel's approval.

6. All user messages:
   - (Ariel, earlier) "lgtm", which merged #890.
   - (Ariel) "I allow upload.wikimedia.org egress. Get teh backgrounds."
   - (Ariel, via coordinator relay, cited verbatim) "Let's talk about the top calendar. The usage flow of this part of the screen is that it starts with presenting all the options of festivals in the world. So first of all, what we need to do is make sure that this doesn't explode with more and more lines because if you have many festivals at the same time, you need extra lines. So first of all, we need to compress all the festivals from a single city or country, I'm not sure either, into one block of festivals that may have an inner presentation of when the festivals take place. But it's very important, the example of Edinburgh, it's very important that all of them will be bunched together. The tooltip on the bunched together uh, should say the number of festivals and the label next to it should say seven festivals including the fringe, where you pick the fringe based on the most shows or something like that. Also, because this allows you to choose festivals, we need to have global awareness. That is, the location of the festival or the festival bunch should be indicated by a flag, a country flag, where that happens, preferably in the middle of the oval, the pill. Next, Indeed, once a user clicks a festival or a festival bunch, the theme is updated behind it, but it's very mild and I want it a little clearer that the ambience changed. Now about the time span, the start and end uh, bars for showing the, the, the planned period look nice on the calendar. And I see on top that it says the amount of days. You need to make the highlighted area draggable. That is, if I want to keep the amount of days but move it a little bit to the side, that shouldn't change the festival selection if there is one. And obviously, clicking on a different festival should change the selection. There's a difference between a click and a drag. Now, below the calendar, there's the explicit first day, number of days, last day, between the getting there and getting home. We don't need that at all. You can put a little label on top of each line that says just the day number. And because there's already the month labels, then you don't need to add more information. Now, the getting there and getting home bits. This is what you didn't understand when I said before. Once the user chooses a festival or a block of time on this calendar, we can imply that the start of the trip and the end of the trip visually on the calendar are not yet set because you don't know how you're getting there. So on the on the calendar itself, just right of the glyph for the draggable bar, on either side of the tour, vacation, sorry, we put a large, like three or four line high icon of, let's say, a plane. And as I said before, it alters between a plane, a train, uh, a home, a car. And because it switches all the time, the user gets the sensation that, OK, I need to click this to set it. And when they click it to set it, first of all, we can ask them, hey, where do you live? We're guessing based on the IP, but where are you coming and where are you going from this trip? And then after they choose that, if they choose that they live there, obviously we don't recommend a flight. But if they don't, we can... give them the option of a flight or a train or a car. And once they choose that, that logo on the calendar is set. It doesn't flick between the, the options and it is static. And by that, we both saved the height of the bar that you put under the, the calendar. And we help the user understand what this is. It's just after the trip that I'm planning, or it's just before the trip that I'm planning. Obviously, it's the transportation. Now, if there's a problem about the shoving the logo between the bar and the end of the screen, don't fight it, because there's always the other side. Either way, both these buttons, before and after the trip, get to the same place of helping the user decide transportation two-way."

7. Pending Tasks:
   - Read the 4 queued GitHub notifications on #900 (CI results, likely) and act. A red CI on #900 means a pushed fix or a PR comment.
   - Wait for Ariel's approval of the re-rendered goldens and "lgtm", then merge #900 with the merge-to-main skill (squash, capture-log).

8. Current Work:
   - Commits ae525b3 (spec) and c6126b3 (implementation plus goldens) are pushed to `claude/project-thread-n6j0dm`.
   - PR #900 is ready for review and subscribed.
   - I replied to Ariel with five screenshots from /mnt/project-files/year-strip-900/ and the defaults chosen: the lane under the rows, grouping by city, and the lead as the festival with a programme and the longest run.
   - The status checklist's last line: "**✓ Pushed and marked the PR ready; CI running**".
   - Four GitHub notifications for #900 have just arrived.

9. Optional Next Step:
